scenes.headline: Decorators
scenes.subtitle: Wrapping functions to add behavior
scenes.narration: Decorators let you layer behavior like logging, timing, or automatic retries onto a function without ever touching its body, keeping cross-cutting concerns clean and reusable.

scenes.headline: The core idea
items: A decorator takes a function, returns one
scenes.narration: In Python, functions are first-class objects, meaning you can pass them around and return them just like any other value. A decorator exploits this by accepting a function and returning a new function that wraps it with extra behavior. The @ syntax is simply convenient sugar for that wrapping step. This pattern shines for cross-cutting concerns you'd otherwise repeat in every function.

scenes.headline: A timing decorator
scenes.narration: The timed decorator defines an inner wrapper that records a start time, calls the original function through fn, then prints how long it took before returning the result. Using args and kwargs means it works with any function signature. The functools.wraps decorator on the wrapper copies over the original function's name and docstring, so introspection still reports the real function rather than the wrapper.

scenes.headline: Applying it
scenes.narration: Placing @timed above extract applies the decorator, and as the comment notes, that line is exactly equivalent to reassigning extract to the result of calling timed on it. From this point on, the name extract refers to the wrapped version, so every call is transparently timed with no change to how you invoke it.

scenes.headline: Decorator flow
scenes.narration: When you call the decorated function, control first enters the wrapper. The wrapper runs its pre-work, then invokes the original function, then runs any post-work such as logging the elapsed time, and finally returns the original's result to the caller. Every call now flows through this envelope.

scenes.text: Always use @functools.wraps on the wrapper so the original name, docstring, and signature survive.
scenes.narration: Always apply functools.wraps to your wrapper so the original function's name, docstring, and signature survive, keeping debuggers and documentation tools accurate.
